I wanted to ask the minister if I understood him rightly in saying that no provision would be made by the government with respect to unemployment for the next year, or for the contingency of unemployment. I did not quite catch his answer on that point.

We are not asking the
government to vote any money at this time on account of possible unemployment for the future or for the present.

Is there any provision for unemployment should the situation require assistance in any portion of Canada, or has the government decided to leave that question in the hands of the provincial governments?

We do not anticipate any condition of unemployment that will warrant the participation of the federal government, either now or in the immediate future, and therefore parliament is not being asked to vote any more money on that account. We think that "Day by day, in every way Canada is getting better and better."
The United States is relieving the minister of very much trouble in that regard.	*
Yes, and no other one gentleman in the Dominion of Canada is more responsible for that fact than is my right hon. friend.
For the policy?

We find my right hon. friend, the leader of a once great party, who is accepting 814,000 of the people's money, standing on the floor of parliament the other night and making the statement, which Hansard will show, that children are dying, and that many suffered and died during the past winter. The statement is absolutely exaggerated and absolutely unfair to Canada, and it is just such statements as that on the part of my right hon. friend, and others like him, that are giving workmen the belief that this Dominion is not a proper country to live in and driving them out to seek employment elsewhere. My right hon. friend is the best advertising medium that Uncle Sam has today in taking from Canada the good citizens that know and love the country and would like to remain here if they were only given a square deal. No immigration agent that the United States ever sent to Regina-as we heard of the other night-or to any other part of the Dominion has been able to do as effective and splendid work in the nature of disgusting Canadians with their own country and turning them loose to seek their fortunes elsewhere as my right hon. friend has done. He can take the chief credit to himself of being the best immigration officer that Uncle Sam has on this continent at the present time.

I appear to have started something. I must say that these fine orations from the Minister of Labour are rather diverting. My latest crime is that I stated in the House, I think three weeks ago, that because of the position we found ourselves in last winter in respect of the coal needs of the poor there had been deaths of children. That is true.
Will my right hon. friend please read the exact language he used.

Read it? Does the
minister think I carry the newspapers of the country around with me?
Oh no, read Hansard.

Oh, Hansard? That u what I stated and that is what appears in Hansard, that children had died, and there have been a lot of deaths, because of inability to provide fuel under the conditions which have prevailed during this last hard winter. The minister says that is an awful thing to say, and that it is the cause of the denudation of the cities of this country by our artisan population who have gone to the United States. Well, I do not like to be disrespectful but I think if the consummation of nonsense was ever reached in the world's history it was reached in this last sentence. The men have gone there by the thousands because there is no work. It is unfortunate. I drew attention to it during the debate on the Address, and I stated that I did not attribute the condition wholly to this government, if at all. These things follow in cycles from world conditions and special conditions in the

country, in respect to which the ^government has only partial control. But I do hold the government responsible for some of the unfortunate circumstances that exist to-day. A government policy can have a substantial effect in curing a situation. No word of pessimism as to this country has ever escaped my lips in this House or in the Dominion.
Nonsense.

The leaders of hon. gentlemen opposite in 1921 declared to the world that we were in the throes of bankruptcy, that even our own men were getting frightened, that we owed so much we could not maintain any longer our integrity as a country; and then they wonder that they did not have any immigration in 1922. No prophecies of that kind or of any kind have been made by me. I am not afraid to state conditions as they exist and as I know them.

Did the right hon. member not, on various platforms in October and November of 1921, prophesy with loud acclaim that if certain things happened the factories of the various towns and cities of Ontario and Canada would be closed?
Surely.

And that the workmen
would be out of work?
Yes.
Was it true?

Yes, certainly it was
true, but hon. gentlemen took care that these things did not happen, at the expense of their plighted word. Undoubtedly it was true. If we had seventeen classes of articles on the free list to-day there would be scores of factories in this Dominion closed beyond any * question, and no one knows it better than the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding). That is what I stated, and hon. gentlemen opposite now point to the factories which are open and say, "Look at them, the prophecies of Mr. Meighen have proved false by the events." No, what proved false was the government. These hon. gentlemen proved false to what they pledged themselves to do in this couhtry, and then they boast of their own duplicity, and point to the condition of the country under the policy now in effect.

This is very entertaining,
but we are not getting very far with the estimates.

The question I asked a *
moment ago was turned into an occasion for a declamation by the minister. Now I seek fMr. Meighen.]
full information. I am trying to find out from the government if it is their policy to leave the solution of the question of unemployment with the provinces. The minister has told us that it is not anticipated that there, will be unemployment. I ask the question purely with a desire to get information, in order that the people in that province who are interested will know, when the crisis arises, where they must go to find employment.

On the 22nd day of December last, after very careful consideration by the government, a telegram was sent to the Prime Minister of British Columbia and a similar telegram to the Prime Minister of Manitoba, in answer to representations they had made to this federal government on the question of unemployment, indicating to these Prime Ministers the view that there was no general condition of unemployment in effect comparable in any way to that in effect during the two preceding winters, and no condition of unemployment which, in the judgment of the government, would warrant the participation of the federal government in a joint unemployment relief scheme such as had been in effect during the past two winters, the telegram indicating, as orders in council had previously indicated, that the question of unemployment relief was primarily One of municipal and provincial concern. The government has maintained that position on the general question of unemployment since that time, and, as a matter of fact, we have seen no great reason for changing that position. So far as British Columbia is concerned, I do not at this moment recall any word that we have received from authorities in British Columbia taking exception to that declaration of our position. It is true that in Manitoba we have received from the Mayor of Winnipeg, and various other representative gentlemen in that province, numerous requests indicating their desire that we should participate in assisting to relieve the conditions of unemployment which it was stated were in effect in Winnipeg. We did not however believe that it was advisable or necessary that the federal government should participate in any unemployment relief scheme, with, of course, one exception provided for in Order No. 220 which was laid on the Table of the House some time ago and which provides that where in certain municipalities relief organizations, composed in part of charitable and soldier organizations with representatives of the municipality, were participating in the relief of unemployed returned men, the federal government would, under the conditions recited in the

Wreck of Alaskan
order in council, pay one-third of the expenditure. Under that order in council we paid out some few thousand dollars, probably not more than ten thousand dollars, since the order in council was passed some weeks ago. Our view is that the conditions which I have just referred to are going to improve rather than get worse, and that there is no necessity at this time, for us to consider such a question as asking for money with which to deal with unemployment, which we do not believe will be general in effect.
